Gian Lorenzo Bernini. The Italian Baroque sculptor and architect who dominated seventeenth-century Rome, defining the Baroque aesthetic through movement, drama, and sensory richness. His marble figures seem to writhe with psychological intensity and theatrical energy, while his architectural commissions reshaped the papal capital.

Bernini sculpted Apollo and Daphne between 1622 and 1625, a marble group capturing the moment of metamorphosis in exquisite detail and movement. He created his David between 1623 and 1624—a muscular, tense figure about to hurl a stone, offering a dynamic reinterpretation of Michelangelo's iconic statue. Bernini designed the baldachin, or canopy, over the altar of Saint Peter's Basilica, a bronze structure combining architecture and sculpture in theatrical grandeur. He was a master of marble drapery, capable of rendering cloth so delicate it seems almost weightless and ethereal.

As an architect as well as a sculptor, Bernini designed the Piazza San Pietro colonnades, urban spaces, and church façades that define Rome's Baroque silhouette. He worked as the principal artist for multiple popes, wielding enormous influence over papal commissions. Apollo and Daphne remains his most virtuosic single work, epitomizing Baroque drama and showing how he surpassed the Renaissance master Michelangelo in dramatic intensity.
